title: Cursor's Breach Started With a Vendor's Leaked Key
author: Rohan Tech official
summary: On November 13, Cursor published the full story behind its October security incident — and the first domino fell outside Cursor's own walls. An access key Cursor had issued to its inference vendor, Fireworks AI, was exposed at Fireworks. The attacker used it to copy coding-agent traces out of a storage bucket the two companies shared. The bucket was read-only, and most of the traces in it dated from 2025, from sessions that weren't running in Privacy Mode. The traces were the real problem Here's the uncomfortable bit: some of those traces held credentials that had never been redacted. The attacker found them, and those credentials opened the door to Cursor's internal SaaS tools. On October 29, that access was used to plant modified copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension — versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 — in the cache behind Cursor's extension marketplace. The tampered builds sat there for about 11 hours, and Cursor says up to 5,000 users may have received them. Anthropic didn't publish those copies; they were slipped in through the compromised access. Where things stand now Cursor says the incident is contained. The last attacker activity it saw was on November 1, and it was blocked. The Fireworks key has been revoked, all inference traffic has moved off Fireworks, and the marketplace has been rebuilt. You can read Cursor's own account in its post, An update on our recent security incident . The takeaway for anyone building with coding agents? Your session traces can hold live secrets, and your model vendors are part of your attack surface whether you planned for it or not. I wrote up the full timeline, the response steps, and what developers should check in the complete piece here: Cursor Traces Its Security Breach to a Fireworks Key

title: Gemini 4 Carbon Just Took the Math Crown From OpenAI
author: Rohan Tech official
summary: The MathArena leaderboard has a new name at the top, and for once it isn't an OpenAI model. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon scored 85.4% expected performance on MathArena with reasoning set to "high", edging out Claude Fable 5.2 (82.8%) and GPT-6.1 Sol (80.6%). Benchmark operator Jasper Dekoninck announced the result on X on Nov 13, and both Sundar Pichai and Demis Hassabis reposted it — a fair sign of how much this one matters internally at Google. Why it stands out MathArena scores models on hard mathematical reasoning, and "expected performance" rewards consistency across the problem set rather than one lucky solve. OpenAI models have held the No. 1 spot for a long stretch, so a 2.6-point lead for a rival is a genuine shift, not noise. The expensive part There's a catch hiding in the cost column. Per the benchmark coverage, Carbon spent roughly $15.70 per problem to get that score. Sol managed its 80.6% for about $1.07 per problem . Nearly fifteen times the spend for under five points of extra performance. That doesn't erase the result — leaderboards measure what a model can do. But if you're planning to run reasoning models at scale, the cost per problem is the number that decides what actually ships. What to watch Can Carbon hold the top spot when the next rival models land? And can Google cut the cost without giving the points back? Reasoning at "high" is clearly where the score came from, so efficiency is where this fight goes next. I broke down the full result, the leaderboard, and what it means for the frontier race here: Gemini 4 Carbon Tops MathArena

title: Nonprofits Sue OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta and SpaceX to Halt Advanced AI Development
author: Rohan Tech official
summary: The AI race now has a court date to worry about. On November 12, a coalition of nonprofit organisations sued OpenAI, Anthropic, Alphabet's Google, Meta and SpaceX's AI division in San Francisco, asking a court to bar further development of the companies' most advanced AI models. The Economic Times reported the filing on November 14. Who is suing, and what do they want? The plaintiffs include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and the Heat Initiative — public-interest and advocacy groups, not commercial rivals. They aren't chasing a settlement cheque. They're asking a judge to press pause on frontier AI development itself, which is about as sweeping a request as a court can receive. The awkward part for the defendants Much of the case rests on the industry's own words. The lawsuit points to public warnings about AI risk made by the companies' own leaders — statements about loss of control and the need for guardrails that were delivered from keynote stages over the past few years. Those quotes are now sitting in a legal filing, and the defendants will have to explain why warnings that sounded serious on stage shouldn't be taken seriously in court. A quick reality check: a lawsuit is an allegation, not a ruling. Nothing in the filing has been proven, and no court has ordered anyone to stop building anything. Why this one stands out AI companies have been sued plenty of times — over training data, copyright and contracts. This case is different in aim. It targets the development of the models themselves, and it arrives while the industry is spending at a scale that would have sounded fictional a few years ago, with new model launches landing almost weekly. Can a court actually freeze frontier AI work at five of the biggest labs on the planet? The groups face a steep climb, and the companies are expected to push back hard. But the filing alone shifts the debate: the industry's own risk language is now evidence in someone else's case. I covered the full story, including what the groups are asking for and what happens next, on Rohan Tech Official: Nonprofits Sue OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta and SpaceX to Halt Advanced AI Development

title: The FAA Ground Stop Wasn't an AI Failure. It Was a Warning.
author: Max Quimby
summary: On Friday, November 13, 2026, at 3:54 p.m. EST, the FAA ordered every departing flight in the United States to stop . For four hours and twenty-one minutes, the third nationwide ground stop in American aviation history played out across all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Nearly 8,000 flights were canceled. More than 10,000 were delayed. European departures to the U.S. were suspended across 42 Eurocontrol member states. Amtrak's call center buckled under sudden demand. 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap → Three days earlier, on November 10, the FAA had expanded its AI-powered SMART routing tool — built by Air Space Intelligence under an $875 million, 12-year contract — to every air traffic control center in the country. The internet had its verdict before the investigation started. What Actually Happened The FAA's official statement cited "communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was more specific: air traffic control routers became overloaded with data and started giving inconsistent readings. The problem originated with what the Wall Street Journal later identified as a single router in southern Arkansas, installed by L3Harris Technologies as part of a copper-to-fiber upgrade program. View the FAA's full statement → That router, according to Reuters reporting , sent roughly a thousand connection attempts every few seconds to other routers in the network — flooding a telecommunications backbone that still runs partly on analog infrastructure. The newer digital equipment kept running. The older systems did not. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford noted that the router explanation was "not a full account of the root cause." The investigation remains open. ℹ️ The ground stop was only the third nationwide halt in U.S. history — after September 11, 2001, and the January 2023 NOTAM system outage caused by accidental file deletion. Over 3,500 aircraft were already airborne when the stop was issued; all landed safely. Exceptions were made for medical flights, critical cargo, and law enforcement. The AI Question Nobody Could Resist Within hours of the ground stop, a parallel narrative took hold: the FAA's new AI tool did this. CNN aviation analyst Mary Schiavo — a former Inspector General of the U.S. Department of Transportation — told CNN : "I don't know if they're linked, but it's just too much of a coincidence that they're trying to start that moving today." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin initially refused to rule out a connection, telling reporters that investigators were still examining whether the AI expansion and the communication failure were related. View the full Mediaite article → The denials came swiftly. Duffy stated: "There's no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened." Air Space Intelligence posted on X that "the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system." The AvWeb coverage confirmed Duffy's claim that SMART "isn't connected to the STARS or ERAM systems" — the core radar and automation platforms that actually route aircraft. View original post on X → So the AI didn't do it. But the fact that everyone assumed it did tells us something important. What SMART Actually Is (And Isn't) SMART — Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — is not an autopilot for the national airspace. It is a cloud-based advisory platform that ingests roughly 200 data streams (weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, airport capacity, controller staffing metrics) and flags likely congestion before aircraft depart. The key architectural detail: SMART generates recommendations. Human air traffic managers review every one. Local facility leaders decide whether to act on them. The system cannot issue clearances, cannot communicate with aircraft, and cannot override controller decisions. Air Space Intelligence built SMART on top of its Flyways AI platform, which is already in operational use with Alaska Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and the U.S. Air Force. The company beat out Palantir Technologies and Thales SA for the FAA contract, awarded in June 2026 . ASI CEO Phillip Buckendorf told NPR : "The machine never makes a decision. It is a human operator, the air traffic manager." 💡 For developers working on AI advisory systems: SMART's architecture is a textbook example of "human-in-the-loop" design. Every recommendation passes through human review before reaching operations. This didn't stop the public from blaming it when something went wrong nearby. The Real Problem: A Tesla Autopilot on a Model T Here is where the dominant narratives both miss the point. Camp one says "AI caused the crash." Wrong. The evidence points to a misbehaving router from a fiber upgrade, not SMART. Camp two says "AI had nothing to do with it." Technically correct. But it glosses over the environment SMART was deployed into. The FAA's telecommunications infrastructure is a patchwork of systems spanning decades. Some facilities still use analog copper lines alongside modern fiber. When Duffy asked Congress for $50 billion on top of the $12.5 billion already approved for modernization, he was acknowledging what every air traffic controller already knew: the backbone is brittle. Deploying a cloud-based AI advisory layer onto infrastructure this fragile is like installing collision-avoidance software in a car whose brakes work intermittently. The software might be flawless. The integration environment is not. View the full CNN live coverage → This matters because the failure mode that actually occurred — a new piece of hardware overwhelming older systems with connection requests — is precisely the kind of cascading failure that happens when you modernize infrastructure piecemeal. New components talk faster and louder than old components can handle. The router that caused Friday's outage wasn't SMART, but it was part of the same modernization push. And SMART's expansion to all 22 centers on November 10 was another piece of that same push. ⚠️ The contrarian take nobody is making: even if SMART is blameless this time, the FAA's modernization approach — deploying new systems onto decades-old infrastructure without replacing the foundation first — guarantees that the next failure will look just like this one. The question isn't whether AI will eventually be in the blast radius. It's when. The Warnings That Were Ignored The timing problem goes deeper than three days. Consider the sequence: June 2026: FAA awards ASI the $875 million SMART contract, beating Palantir and Thales. September 21, 2026: SMART begins limited operations in Washington, D.C. airspace. On the same day, a blown circuit at Philadelphia TRACON triggers ground stops at JFK, Newark, and Philadelphia. The FAA attributes it to equipment failure, not SMART. October 9, 2026: More than two dozen House lawmakers ask the FAA to pause SMART, citing the lack of a published safety evaluation. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) says it "has not been involved in the design, testing, or implementation of SMART." October 2026: Airlines including Delta and American back the tool but warn that a rapid transition could cause unnecessary cancellations. November 10: SMART expanded to all 22 centers. November 13: Nationwide ground stop. Read the full IVN analysis → The IVN analysis frames this well: causation is unproven, but the coincidence and the unanswered warnings make the rollout a legitimate subject for oversight, whatever the investigation finds. The Integration Risk Spectrum For AI builders deploying into critical infrastructure — healthcare, energy, transportation, finance — Friday's ground stop is your case study. Not because the AI failed, but because it took the blame anyway. Level 1 — Isolated Advisory: The AI system runs on completely separate infrastructure, communicates through well-defined interfaces, and cannot affect host system operations even if it fails catastrophically. SMART claims to be here. Level 2 — Shared Resources: The AI system shares some infrastructure (network, compute, storage) with the host system. A failure in the AI system could compete for resources with the host. This is where many enterprise AI deployments actually land. Level 3 — Integrated Operations: The AI system's outputs directly feed into operational workflows, even if humans approve each one. Latency, availability, or data quality issues in the AI system degrade the host system's performance. Level 4 — Autonomous Control: The AI system makes decisions without human review. Aviation regulators have explicitly stated this is not where SMART sits, and it is not where any current air traffic AI sits. The lesson from November 13: even a Level 1 system gets blamed when it shares an institutional context with a failure. And if SMART's deployment timeline is later found to have created any shared infrastructure dependencies — even indirectly — it moves to Level 2 territory, where the risk calculus changes entirely. What the Community Is Saying The public reaction split along predictable lines. On Reddit, the story drew massive engagement, with commenters split between "this is why you don't let AI run critical infrastructure" and "read the article — the AI didn't cause this." The more technically literate discussions focused on the infrastructure angle: aging FAA systems, the L3Harris router issue, and whether the $50 billion modernization ask was realistic. View the full Hacker News discussion → Read the full AvWeb coverage → On the policy side, Rep. Don Beyer called for an end to AI in air traffic control entirely. Sen. Tammy Duckworth and Rep. Ted Lieu demanded hearings. The political incentive structure is clear: blaming AI is bipartisan catnip. Nobody loses votes for being cautious about "robots controlling planes," even when the robots in question are spreadsheets with better data. Major news outlets rapidly covered the story as it unfolded, with ABC News among the first to report the ground stop's sweeping impact on travelers nationwide. View original post on X → The National Weather Service even had to step in, posting on X that reports of a nationwide radar outage were false — outdated webpages were circulating as if they were live. View original post on X → Former controller Dave Riley told NPR he thinks the FAA is "overstating the impact of this software tool." Airlines for America, the industry trade group, praised the modernization push. The controllers' union wants a seat at the table it was never given. What This Means for You If you are building AI systems that touch critical infrastructure — healthcare, energy, transportation, finance — Friday's ground stop is your case study. Not because the AI failed, but because it took the blame anyway. Three takeaways for AI builders in regulated domains: Build your isolation proof before you ship. Document, with architectural diagrams, exactly which infrastructure your system shares with the host environment. If you share a network segment, a database, or even a deployment timeline with legacy systems, you are in the blast radius when those systems fail. ASI's defense was clean — SMART isn't connected to STARS or ERAM. Make sure you can say the same. Treat deployment timing as a risk variable. Expanding to all 22 centers three days before a catastrophic infrastructure failure created a narrative problem that no amount of technical evidence will fully resolve. Phased rollouts with documented checkpoints between phases are not just good engineering — they are your legal and public-relations defense. The "human in the loop" defense has limits. SMART's architecture is genuinely human-in-the-loop. Every recommendation goes through human review. This did not stop the public, the media, or members of Congress from treating it as an autonomous system that crashed the national airspace. If your system is advisory, make the human decision points visible and auditable — not just technically present. ℹ️ Related reading: When AI model outages become single points of failure and The AI liability fight nobody wants to have . Looking Forward The investigation is ongoing. The L3Harris router explanation may hold, or it may be a partial account — Bedford's caution suggests the FAA itself is not fully satisfied. Congress will hold hearings. The $50 billion funding ask will become a political football. But regardless of the investigation's conclusion, the pattern is set. AI systems deployed into critical infrastructure will be blamed for failures they did not cause, defended by technical arguments the public cannot evaluate, and regulated by lawmakers who do not distinguish between advisory and autonomous systems. The builders who survive this environment will not be the ones with the best AI. They will be the ones who understood that deploying into critical infrastructure means your system is guilty until proven innocent — and who built their architecture, their documentation, and their deployment process accordingly. SMART may well prove to be exactly what the FAA needs. But on November 13, what mattered was not what the AI did. It was what everybody assumed. Originally published at ComputeLeap
